title: Molecular Biology
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned 300L Biology molecular biology curriculum: DNA replication mechanics, transcription and RNA processing, the genetic code and translation, prokaryotic and eukaryotic gene regulation, recombinant DNA techniques, and common molecular biology laboratory methods.

questions.question: The central dogma of molecular biology describes the general flow of genetic information as:
options: DNA directly to protein without an RNA intermediate
questions.correct_answer: DNA to RNA to protein
questions.explanation: The central dogma states that genetic information generally flows from DNA, which is transcribed into RNA, which is then translated into protein.

questions.question: At the replication fork, DNA polymerase synthesises the leading strand continuously, while the lagging strand is synthesised discontinuously as short fragments called:
questions.correct_answer: Okazaki fragments
questions.explanation: Because DNA polymerase only synthesises 5' to 3', the lagging strand is made in short discontinuous Okazaki fragments that are later joined by DNA ligase.

questions.question: Which enzyme unwinds the DNA double helix ahead of the replication fork by breaking hydrogen bonds between base pairs?
questions.correct_answer: Helicase
questions.explanation: Helicase uses ATP hydrolysis to unwind the double helix at the replication fork, separating the two parental strands for copying.

questions.question: Primase is required during DNA replication because:
options: DNA polymerase cannot begin synthesis without a free 3'-OH group provided by a short RNA primer
It relieves supercoiling ahead of the replication fork
questions.correct_answer: DNA polymerase cannot begin synthesis without a free 3'-OH group provided by a short RNA primer
questions.explanation: DNA polymerases can only extend an existing strand, so primase synthesises a short RNA primer that provides the free 3'-OH group needed to begin DNA synthesis.

questions.question: DNA ligase functions in replication and repair by:
options: Sealing nicks in the sugar-phosphate backbone by forming phosphodiester bonds between adjacent fragments
questions.correct_answer: Sealing nicks in the sugar-phosphate backbone by forming phosphodiester bonds between adjacent fragments
questions.explanation: DNA ligase catalyses the formation of a phosphodiester bond to join adjacent Okazaki fragments (after primer removal and gap filling) into a continuous strand.

questions.question: In prokaryotic transcription, the enzyme RNA polymerase binds to a specific DNA sequence to initiate transcription, called the:
questions.correct_answer: Promoter
questions.explanation: The promoter is the DNA sequence upstream of a gene where RNA polymerase (aided by sigma factor in bacteria) binds to initiate transcription.

questions.question: In eukaryotic mRNA processing, the removal of non-coding intron sequences and joining of exons is called:
questions.correct_answer: Splicing
questions.explanation: Splicing, carried out by the spliceosome, removes introns from the pre-mRNA and joins exons together to form mature mRNA.

questions.question: The addition of a 7-methylguanosine cap to the 5' end of eukaryotic pre-mRNA primarily serves to:
options: Protect the mRNA from degradation and aid ribosome binding during translation initiation
Add a poly-A tail to the 3' end
questions.correct_answer: Protect the mRNA from degradation and aid ribosome binding during translation initiation
questions.explanation: The 5' cap protects mRNA from exonuclease degradation and is recognised by translation initiation factors that help recruit the ribosome.

questions.question: The genetic code is described as 'degenerate' because:
options: Some amino acids are specified by more than one codon
Some codons specify no amino acid at all
The code differs completely between all species
Each amino acid has exactly one unique codon
questions.correct_answer: Some amino acids are specified by more than one codon
questions.explanation: Degeneracy (redundancy) of the genetic code means most amino acids are encoded by more than one triplet codon, which helps buffer against some point mutations.

questions.question: Which of the following is a start codon that also codes for the amino acid methionine in most organisms?
questions.correct_answer: AUG
questions.explanation: AUG is the near-universal start codon signalling the beginning of translation and coding for methionine (or formylmethionine in bacteria).

questions.question: The 'wobble hypothesis' explains why:
options: Ribosomes can move along mRNA in either direction
A single tRNA can pair with more than one codon due to flexible base pairing at the third codon position
questions.correct_answer: A single tRNA can pair with more than one codon due to flexible base pairing at the third codon position
questions.explanation: Wobble base pairing allows non-standard pairing at the third position of the codon-anticodon interaction, letting one tRNA recognise multiple synonymous codons.

questions.question: During translation, the ribosomal site where a new incoming aminoacyl-tRNA first binds is called the:
questions.correct_answer: A site
questions.explanation: The A (aminoacyl) site is where each new charged tRNA enters the ribosome to pair with the mRNA codon before peptide bond formation.

questions.question: Translation terminates when the ribosome encounters a stop codon (UAA, UAG, or UGA) because:
options: A special tRNA with an anticodon for the stop codon binds and adds a stop amino acid
No tRNA normally recognises stop codons; instead release factors bind and trigger release of the polypeptide
The ribosome runs out of ATP
RNA polymerase detaches from the DNA
questions.correct_answer: No tRNA normally recognises stop codons; instead release factors bind and trigger release of the polypeptide
questions.explanation: Stop codons are not recognised by tRNAs but by release factors, which promote hydrolysis of the bond between the polypeptide and the tRNA, releasing the finished protein.

questions.question: In the lac operon of E. coli, in the absence of lactose, the lac repressor protein:
options: Binds to the operator and blocks RNA polymerase from transcribing the structural genes
Binds to the promoter and enhances transcription
Activates transcription of the structural genes
questions.correct_answer: Binds to the operator and blocks RNA polymerase from transcribing the structural genes
questions.explanation: Without lactose, the lac repressor binds the operator sequence and sterically blocks RNA polymerase, keeping the lac operon genes (lacZ, lacY, lacA) off.

questions.question: In the lac operon system, allolactose (derived from lactose) induces transcription by:
options: Binding to the lac repressor, changing its shape so it can no longer bind the operator
Binding to the promoter to recruit sigma factor
questions.correct_answer: Binding to the lac repressor, changing its shape so it can no longer bind the operator
questions.explanation: Allolactose acts as an inducer that binds the repressor allosterically, causing it to release the operator and allowing transcription of the lac operon to proceed.

questions.question: The trp operon of E. coli is an example of a repressible operon, meaning that:
options: Transcription is normally off and is switched on by an inducer
Transcription is normally on and is switched off when tryptophan levels are high, acting as a corepressor
It has no regulatory protein at all
It is regulated only by catabolite repression
questions.correct_answer: Transcription is normally on and is switched off when tryptophan levels are high, acting as a corepressor
questions.explanation: In the trp operon, tryptophan itself acts as a corepressor that binds the trp repressor, activating it to bind the operator and shut down transcription when tryptophan is abundant.

questions.question: In eukaryotic gene regulation, enhancers can influence transcription of a gene even though they are located far from the promoter, because:
options: They directly code for the protein
DNA looping brings transcription factors bound at the enhancer into contact with the promoter-bound transcription machinery
They are transcribed into the mRNA itself
They physically move along the chromosome to the promoter
questions.correct_answer: DNA looping brings transcription factors bound at the enhancer into contact with the promoter-bound transcription machinery
questions.explanation: Enhancers work at a distance because the DNA between them and the promoter loops out, allowing enhancer-bound activator proteins to interact directly with the transcription initiation complex.

questions.question: DNA methylation, typically at cytosine bases in CpG islands, generally has which effect on gene expression?
options: It is commonly associated with gene silencing/repression of transcription
It has no known effect on transcription
questions.correct_answer: It is commonly associated with gene silencing/repression of transcription
questions.explanation: DNA methylation of promoter CpG islands is an epigenetic modification generally correlated with transcriptional repression and heterochromatin formation.

questions.question: Restriction endonucleases are enzymes used in recombinant DNA technology because they:
options: Join DNA fragments together at their ends
Cut DNA at specific recognition sequences, producing fragments with defined ends
Synthesise new DNA strands from a template
Amplify DNA exponentially using heat cycling
questions.correct_answer: Cut DNA at specific recognition sequences, producing fragments with defined ends
questions.explanation: Restriction enzymes recognise specific palindromic DNA sequences and cleave the DNA there, generating fragments (often with sticky ends) useful for cloning.

questions.question: In molecular cloning, a plasmid vector must contain which of the following to be useful for selecting bacteria that have taken it up?
options: A selectable marker gene, such as antibiotic resistance
questions.correct_answer: A selectable marker gene, such as antibiotic resistance
questions.explanation: A selectable marker, commonly an antibiotic resistance gene, allows researchers to identify and select only the bacterial cells that have successfully taken up the recombinant plasmid.

questions.question: The polymerase chain reaction (PCR) amplifies a specific DNA segment through repeated cycles of:
questions.correct_answer: Denaturation, primer annealing, and extension
questions.explanation: PCR cycles through heat denaturation to separate DNA strands, cooling to allow primers to anneal, and extension by a heat-stable DNA polymerase (e.g., Taq) to copy the target sequence.

questions.question: Taq polymerase is favoured for PCR because it is:
options: Isolated from a human cell line
A heat-stable DNA polymerase derived from the thermophilic bacterium Thermus aquaticus, able to survive repeated denaturation temperatures
An RNA polymerase that does not require primers
Capable of proofreading and error correction, unlike all other polymerases
questions.correct_answer: A heat-stable DNA polymerase derived from the thermophilic bacterium Thermus aquaticus, able to survive repeated denaturation temperatures
questions.explanation: Taq polymerase, from the thermophile Thermus aquaticus, withstands the high temperatures (around 94-98 degrees Celsius) used to denature DNA in each PCR cycle without being destroyed.

questions.question: Agarose gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments primarily on the basis of:
options: Their size, with smaller fragments migrating faster through the gel matrix toward the positive electrode
Their overall charge to mass ratio, which varies widely among DNA fragments
Their base composition (GC versus AT content) alone
questions.correct_answer: Their size, with smaller fragments migrating faster through the gel matrix toward the positive electrode
questions.explanation: Because DNA has a uniform negative charge per unit length, electrophoresis separates fragments mainly by size as they move through the gel matrix toward the anode, smaller fragments moving faster.

questions.question: The Southern blotting technique is used to detect specific:
questions.correct_answer: DNA sequences
questions.explanation: Southern blotting transfers separated DNA fragments to a membrane and probes for a specific DNA sequence using a labelled complementary probe.

questions.question: Northern blotting is analogous to Southern blotting but is used specifically to detect:
questions.correct_answer: RNA transcripts
questions.explanation: Northern blotting follows the same principle as Southern blotting but is applied to RNA, allowing detection and study of specific gene transcripts.

questions.question: Western blotting is used to detect and analyse specific:
questions.correct_answer: Proteins
questions.explanation: Western blotting uses antibodies to detect specific proteins that have been separated by gel electrophoresis and transferred to a membrane.

questions.question: Sanger (chain-termination) DNA sequencing relies on the incorporation of:
options: Dideoxynucleotides (ddNTPs) lacking a 3'-OH group, which terminate strand elongation when incorporated
Restriction enzymes to cut at every base
questions.correct_answer: Dideoxynucleotides (ddNTPs) lacking a 3'-OH group, which terminate strand elongation when incorporated
questions.explanation: Sanger sequencing mixes normal dNTPs with chain-terminating ddNTPs; incorporation of a ddNTP halts further extension, producing fragments of varying length that reveal the sequence when separated by size.

questions.question: A silent mutation is one in which a nucleotide change:
options: Alters the amino acid sequence of the resulting protein
Does not change the amino acid encoded, usually due to codon degeneracy
questions.correct_answer: Does not change the amino acid encoded, usually due to codon degeneracy
questions.explanation: A silent mutation changes a codon to a synonymous one that still specifies the same amino acid, so the protein sequence is unaffected.

questions.question: A nonsense mutation converts a codon that normally specifies an amino acid into:
options: A stop codon, causing premature termination of translation
questions.correct_answer: A stop codon, causing premature termination of translation
questions.explanation: A nonsense mutation changes a sense codon into a premature stop codon, truncating the resulting polypeptide, usually producing a non-functional protein.

questions.question: Nucleotide excision repair is a DNA repair mechanism primarily used to correct:
options: Single mismatched bases caused by replication errors
Bulky helix-distorting DNA lesions such as thymine dimers caused by UV light
questions.correct_answer: Bulky helix-distorting DNA lesions such as thymine dimers caused by UV light
questions.explanation: Nucleotide excision repair removes a short single-stranded segment containing a bulky lesion, such as a UV-induced pyrimidine dimer, and resynthesises it using the intact complementary strand as template.

questions.question: Mismatch repair systems correct errors that:
options: Occur when DNA polymerase incorporates an incorrect, non-complementary base during replication and it escapes proofreading
Are caused only by ionising radiation
questions.correct_answer: Occur when DNA polymerase incorporates an incorrect, non-complementary base during replication and it escapes proofreading
questions.explanation: Mismatch repair scans newly replicated DNA for base-pairing errors missed by polymerase proofreading and corrects the mismatched base using the parental strand as the reference.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the function of a signal peptide/sequence found on some newly synthesised proteins?
options: It directs the protein to its correct cellular destination, such as the endoplasmic reticulum
It provides the start codon for translation
It codes for a regulatory RNA molecule
questions.correct_answer: It directs the protein to its correct cellular destination, such as the endoplasmic reticulum
questions.explanation: A signal sequence at the N-terminus of a nascent polypeptide is recognised by the signal recognition particle and directs the ribosome-protein complex to the endoplasmic reticulum for further processing.

questions.question: Reverse transcriptase, an enzyme used in molecular biology to synthesise cDNA, catalyses the synthesis of:
questions.correct_answer: DNA from an RNA template
questions.explanation: Reverse transcriptase, originally identified in retroviruses, synthesises complementary DNA (cDNA) using an RNA template, which is widely used to clone expressed genes.
